SOCIAL ANTHROPOLOGY  
UNIT – I  
 
INTRODUCTION  
It is important to know the development and scope of social anthropology as a subject. We 
know social anthropology today has many stages of development. The subject has not 
obtained today’s form overnight. It has many theoretical debates since its emergence and till 
today all the matters of debate have not come to an end. So, it is very much important to the 
students of anthropology to understand these issues and also to know the history related to the 
subject.  
The most common and basic definition of Anthropology is to say that Anthropology is the 
study of man across time and space. Anthropology deals with every aspect of human being. It 
not only studies human beings in present context but also studies human beings’ journey 
through the path of evolution from Pleistocene period till today’s globalised world and tries 
to trace the future path. Anthropology studies man irrespective of any geographical boundary. 
It studies human being as a whole and tries to study differences within it.  
NATURE AND SCOPE OF SOCIAL ANTHROPOLOGY  
Social anthropology aims to study human society. It is a holistic study necessarily and covers 
all parts related to human society. Culture comes naturally under this, as it is an integral part 
of human society. So, the basic aim of social anthropology is to study human being as a 
social animal. Thus, to fulfil its aim it explores, in a broad area, covering almost every aspect 
of human social life. The aim of modern social anthropology is just not to study human 
society but also to understand the complex issues of modern human life. As primitive people 
have been the focus of anthropological study, the problems faced by these people in the 
process of development in modern days become very important for the anthropologists to 
study.  Anthropologists not only deal with the study of these problems but also try to find out 
a solution for this. Developmental anthropology and Action anthropology etc. are the 
specialised fields within social anthropology which deal with such problems. Therefore, we 
can say that the scope and aim of social anthropology go together; one influences the other. 
As much as the scope increases a new aim comes out of it.  
Though we have subjective debate over the term social anthropology and cultural 
anthropology, sometimes we find interchangeable use of these two terms. People use the term 
socio-cultural anthropology to replace these two terms. But historically there is a debate over 
the ideology of these two terms and as a student of anthropology we need to know these 
issues.  
 
Anthropology basically has two dominant schools of thought. One is British school of 
thought, and the other is American school of thought. British school of thought branches out 
Anthropology into three basic branches

1) Biological or physical anthropology.   
2) Social anthropology.   
3) Archaeology.   
American school defines four branches of Anthropology:   
1) Physical anthropology   
2) Cultural anthropology.   
3) Archaeology   
4) Linguistic anthropology.  
Different scholars like S.C. Roy, D.N. Majumdar, G.S. Ghurye, S.C. Dube, N.K. Bose, 
L.P.  Vidyarthi and S. Sinha had tried to find out the genesis and development of Social 
Anthropology in India. S.C. Roy’s paper Anthropological Research in India (1921) reflects 
upon the works on tribes and castes published before 1921. The anthropological accounts 
consisted of the writings of British administrators and missionaries as before 1921 
anthropological work in India was mainly done by these people. After this, D.N. Majumdar 
tried to trace the development of Anthropology in India. This attempt was made after twenty-
five years of S.C. Roy’s work. D.N. Majumdar tried to relate the developing discipline of 
Anthropology in India with the theory of culture that originated in Britain and America. 
American influence was first recognised besides the works of British administrators and 
missionaries.  
 
ANTHROPOLOGICAL PERSPECTIVE  
Anthropology is the study of people, past and present that focuses on understanding the 
human condition both culturally and biologically. Anthropological perspective focuses on the 
study of full scope of human diversity and application of that knowledge to help people of 
different backgrounds.  
 
FOUR MAIN PERSPECTIVE  
1. Cross-Cultural Approach  
2. Evolutionary or Historical Approach  
3. Ecological Approach 
4. Holistic Approach  
Cross-Cultural Approach  
This emphasis also makes anthropology unique among the social sciences. Unlike 
sociologists, psychologists, economists and political scientists, anthropologists look beyond 
the confines of our own society and compare it to the beliefs and practices of other societies, 
past and present. Where a sociologist, for example, may attempt to explain social

organization with reference only to their own society, an anthropologist would almost 
invariably go on to compare our own patterns of social organization with other societies.  
Evolutionary Or Historical Approach  
This approach, coming from archaeology and physical anthropology, focuses upon both the 
biological and cultural evolution of human beings and of human societies. It is also one of the 
reasons why a four subfields approach is so important to the discipline. An 
evolutionary/historical approach is "diachronic." In other words, it is focused upon the 
understanding of and description of patterns of change over time. This approach provides 
time depth to an anthropological perspective which, along with its cross-cultural emphasis, 
helps to put contemporary society and contemporary patterns of social development into an 
historical context.  
Ecological Approach  
Focuses on human societies or cultures within the context of larger natural system. This 
approach is to understand the ecological perspective position of human being and its 
societies.  
Holistic Approach  
This approach focuses on philosophy of functionalism. It is very closely related to an 
ecological approach philosophically. In fact, anthropology was the first social science to 
begin to incorporate ecological insights into its studies of human behaviour and society. 
Ecology has been part of the discipline at least since the 1960s. Anthropology also remains 
the only social science which continues to incorporate ecology in a significant and integral 
way (even though all anthropologists wouldn’t agree that we should be ecological). 
 
GROWTH AND DEVELOPENT OF INDIAN ANTHROPOLOGY  
The course of development of anthropological thought and study in India slow but steady. 
The systematic efforts to unravel the secrets of humanity can be seen since the time of the 
Vedic literature of ancient India. Basu Roy describes the following phases of development of 
Indian Anthropology, while some other anthropologists differ in their opinion regarding the 
time span of these periods.  
1) Formative Phase (1774 – 1919)  
During this period the emphasis of anthropological studies was on tribal life and the diversity 
of their customs in India. Many encyclopaedias on tribes and castes were published. In 
addition to the ethnographic reports, revenue reports of Dalton, Buchanon and Lord Baden 
Powell also examined the social cultural situation in India during this period.  
The foundation of Asiatic Society of India by Sir William Jones in 1774 was an important 
landmark during this period. This became the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784. By this time, 
the society also started publishing its journal regularly.

By 1872, The Indian Antiquary was published. It contained many articles of anthropological 
interests. In 1886, the Anthropological Society of Bombay published its journal. It was the 
first journal, exclusively for anthropology.  
The publication of journals helped to disseminate anthropological outlook in India. In 1912 S 
C Roy published the monograph Munda and their country. The journal of Bihar and Orissa 
Research Society was started in 1915.  
Anthropology had been introduced as subject in the Sociology Department of Bombay 
University in 1919. According to D N Majumdar, the formative phase ended in 1911. 
However, for L P Vidyarti, this period extended up to 1920.  
 
2) The Constructive Phase (1920 – 1949)  
L K Ananthakrishnan Iyer and R Chanda, the pioneers of Indian anthropology, joined the 
department during this phase. Another remarkable step during this period was the publication 
of journal ‘Man in India’ in 1921, under the editorial ship of S C Roy. The 25th Indian 
Science Congress was held at Calcutta in 1938, and the focal theme was ‘Anthropology in 
India’. A joint session of the Indian Science Congress Association and British Association 
reviewed the progress of anthropology in India. This was the first review of the 
anthropological research in India. In 1939, Verrier Elwin published his book The Baiga. In 
this book he had proposed that the tribes should be left alone and they should be allowed to 
develop in isolation, away from the mainstream. The need for a full-fledged anthropological 
research organization was fulfilled by establishing Anthropological Survey of India in 
1945. B S Guha was the first Director of this institution at Calcutta. In 1947, a Department of 
Anthropology was opened in the University of Delhi.  
3) The Analytical Phase (1950 – 1990)  
For D N Majumdar (1950), this phase began in 1938 and carried on to the present. The earlier 
anthropologists like Surjit Sinha, called this, the recent phase. By this time, Indian 
Anthropologists started regularly interacting with foreign anthropologists. Many kinds of 
collaborative works were taken up. Moreover, during this period, there was shift from the 
descriptive studies of preliterate societies to the analytical studies of complex societies.  
Some anthropologists from abroad came to India to conduct research. Their works created a 
momentum to the anthropological research in India. The villages they studied became 
famous. Many village study monographs were published in the 1960s through the Census of 
India 1961. The first of these was a study of Ghaghara by L P Vidyarthi. These studies helped 
to generate new concepts and ideas. The works of L P Vidyarthi, B K Roy, Burman, R M 
Makhan Jha, P K Misra, K S Singh and T N Madan are worth mentioning.  
4) Evaluative Phase (1990 to the present)  
During recent times new areas of Anthropology and different sub-fields within these areas 
have been emergence. Interest in Medical Anthropology, Religion, Development studies and 
psychological studies are more evident. Numerous papers have been published by 
anthropologists in India concerning

(a) change leading to tribal identity, integration, vanishing culture and planning, (b) 
emergence of Industrial Anthropology,   
(c) increased emphasis on tribal demography   
(d) Integrated study of tribal regions.   
Important contributions have been made to Action Research, Socio- Psychological Research, 
and Folk-lore researchers. Studies of Power structure and Leadership and Anthropology of 
Religion.  
To conclude in the words of L P Vidyarthi. “The journey of Indian Anthropology still 
Continues”.  It has gone much ahead under the influence of and in collaboration with the 
British and American anthropologists. Of course, in a broader perspective, they will continue 
to influence the Indian social science for some more time. Anthropology originated a little 
late. But today it has become an important discipline all over the world. This subject taught in 
almost all renowned universities with greater importance. In some western countries, apart 
from anthropological institutions, anthropologists are appointed in various other areas as 
well. Thus, anthropology occupies a significant position and holds a great relevance in the 
modern world.  
Features of Tribes and Concept of Tribe–Caste Continuum in India 
India is a country of enormous social and cultural diversity. Along with caste, class, 
religion and language groups, tribal communities form an important part of Indian society. 
Tribes have their own traditions, customs, social institutions, languages, occupations and 
cultural practices. The study of tribes is important for understanding social diversity, 
inclusion, development, empowerment and social change in India. 
CONCEPT OF TRIBE 
The word tribe generally refers to a social group whose members share a common territory, 
culture, traditions, language, customs and a sense of collective identity. 
In the Indian context, tribal communities are officially recognised as Scheduled Tribes (STs) 
under the Constitution. 
A tribe traditionally tends to have: 
 
A common geographical area  
 
Common culture and traditions  
 
A shared language or dialect  
 
Strong community feeling  
 
Distinct social customs  
 
Traditional occupations  
 
A sense of common identity

Simple Example 
Imagine a community living in a forest or hilly region for generations. Most members follow 
similar customs, celebrate common festivals, speak a local dialect and have traditional 
systems for resolving disputes. Such characteristics help us understand the traditional concept 
of a tribal community. 
 Major Features of Tribes 
 Common Territory: Traditionally, tribal communities have been closely associated 
with a particular geographical area. They may inhabit forest regions, hills, mountains, 
Plateaus and Remote rural areas. Example: Many tribal communities in central India 
have historically depended upon forests for food, fuel, medicine and livelihood. 
 Common Culture: Tribal communities generally possess distinctive cultural 
practices. These may include traditional dress, food habits, folk songs, folk dances, 
festivals, rituals, marriage customs, religious practices and Art and crafts. Example: 
The Gond and Warli communities are well known for distinctive artistic traditions. 
 
Common Language or Dialect: Many tribal communities have their own languages 
or dialects. Language plays an important role in maintaining cultural identity, oral 
traditions, folk knowledge, stories and myths and community relationships. However, 
many tribal people are also multilingual and use regional languages for education, 
employment and interaction with non-tribal populations. 
 
Strong Sense of Community: A strong feeling of collective identity is traditionally 
associated with tribal societies. Members often cooperate in agriculture, festivals, 
community activities, social ceremonies, conflict resolution and resource management  
 
Tribal Religion and Beliefs: Traditional tribal belief systems often include strong 
connections with nature, ancestors, spirits, mountains, rivers, forests and animals. 
 
Distinctive Art and Cultural Expressions: Tribal communities have contributed 
significantly to India's cultural heritage. Examples include Tribal paintings, Jewellery 
Woodcraft, Bamboo craft, pottery, folk music and dance.

UNIT-I 
LONG QUESTIONS 
1. Define Social Anthropology and discuss its nature, scope and major areas of study. Explain 
the importance of the holistic and comparative approaches in understanding human 
society.  
2. Discuss the relationship between Social Anthropology and Sociology. Explain their 
similarities, differences, approaches and areas of overlap with suitable examples.  
3. Explain the major anthropological perspectives used in the study of human society. 
Discuss the cross-cultural, evolutionary/historical, ecological and holistic approaches in 
detail.  
4. Define the concept of tribe and discuss the major characteristics of tribal communities. 
Explain the importance of common territory, culture, language, community feeling, 
customs and traditional occupations in tribal life.  
5. Discuss the growth and development of Social Anthropology in India. Explain the major 
phases of Indian Anthropology and highlight the contributions of important Indian 
anthropologists.  
6. Explain the concept of Tribe–Caste Continuum in India. Discuss how tribal and caste 
communities may show similarities, differences and processes of social interaction and 
cultural change.

UNIT-2  
Introduction – What is Social Anthropology? 
Meaning 
The word anthropology comes from two Greek words: anthropos (human being) and logos 
(study or science). So, anthropology means "the study of human beings". It studies humans in 
the widest possible way – their bodies, their past, their languages and their ways of life. 
Social Anthropology is the branch that studies human society and culture: how people live 
together, form families, earn a living, exchange goods, follow religion, obey rules and organise 
power. Instead of asking "how does one person behave?", it asks, "how do groups of people 
behave, and why do they behave in these ways?". 
Main branches of Anthropology 
Branch 
What it studies 
Simple example 
Physical (Biological) 
Anthropology 
Human evolution, body types, genetics 
Why do people differ in skin colour 
or height? 
Archaeological 
Anthropology 
Past societies through tools, ruins and 
remains 
Life in the Indus Valley from 
excavated objects 
Linguistic Anthropology 
Language and how it shapes thought 
How do tribal languages describe 
kinship? 
Social / Cultural 
Anthropology 
Living societies, customs, institutions 
Marriage rules among the Santhals; 
trade among Trobriand islanders 
 
Social anthropology and cultural anthropology are remarkably close. In Britain the term social 
anthropology is preferred (focus on social relations and structure). In the USA the term cultural 
anthropology is preferred (focus on beliefs, values and symbols). In these notes we treat them 
together. 
Important characteristics  
• Holistic approach: it studies a society as a whole – economy, religion, family, politics – 
because all parts are linked. 
• Comparative method: it compares many societies to find common patterns and real 
differences. 
• Fieldwork: the anthropologist lives among the people, learns their language and 
observes daily life (this is called participant observation). 
• Cultural relativism: every culture should be understood in its own terms, not judged as 
"good" or "bad" by our standards.

• Emic and etic views: the emic view is the "insider's" understanding; the etic view is the 
"outsider's" scientific description. 
 
Origin of Social Anthropology 
 Early roots 
Curiosity about "other people" is very old. Ancient Greek writers such as Herodotus (often 
called the "Father of History") described the customs of Egyptians, Persians and Scythians. 
Chinese, Arab and Indian travellers also left accounts. Ibn Khaldun (14th century) wrote about 
how societies rise and fall, and Al-Biruni wrote a famous study of India in the 11th century. 
But these were travel accounts, not organised science. 
Why did anthropology begin as a science in the 19th century? 
1. Age of exploration and colonial expansion: European traders, missionaries and 
administrators met people in Africa, Asia, the Americas and the Pacific whose ways of 
life looked very different. Europeans wanted to understand them – partly out of 
curiosity, partly to govern and trade with them. 
2. Darwin's theory of evolution (1859): On the Origin of Species changed how people 
thought about living things. Scholars began asking whether human societies also 
"evolve" step by step. 
3. The Enlightenment and belief in reason: thinkers believed society could be studied 
scientifically, like nature. 
4. Growth of other social sciences: sociology (Comte, Spencer, Durkheim), history and 
economics gave methods and ideas. 
5. Museums and collections: objects, tools and photographs brought from colonies created 
material to study. 
Three stages in the growth of the subject 
• Stage 1 – Speculative or "armchair" stage (c. 1850–1900): scholars sat in libraries and 
built grand theories from reports of travellers and missionaries. Evolutionism and 
Diffusionism belong here. 
• Stage 2 – Fieldwork stage (c. 1900–1950): anthropologists went to live among the 
people. Functionalism dominated. Emphasis on detail and direct observation. 
• Stage 3 – Theoretical diversification (c. 1950 onwards): Structuralism, symbolic 
anthropology, Marxist and feminist approaches, and interpretive anthropology 
appeared.

Meaning of Evolutionism 
Evolutionism (also called Classical Evolutionism or Unilineal Evolutionism) is the theory that 
all human societies pass through the same series of stages in the same order – from simple to 
complex, from "primitive" to "civilised". It was the first major theory of social anthropology 
and dominated the second half of the 19th century. 
Think of the growth of a human being: infant → child → adult. Evolutionists believed societies 
also grow in a fixed sequence. Just as every person passes through childhood, every society 
was thought to pass through early stages of hunting, herding, farming and finally industrial 
civilisation. 
Basic ideas (assumptions) 
• Psychic unity of mankind: the human mind works in basically the same way 
everywhere. So, people in different places, facing similar problems, invent similar 
solutions independently. 
• Unilineal (single line) development: there is one main path of progress that all societies 
follow. 
• Progress: societies move from simple to complex, from lower to higher forms. 
• Comparative method: by placing present-day "simple" societies on the ladder of stages, 
we can reconstruct the past of "advanced" societies. Today's tribes were seen as "living 
fossils". 
• Survivals: customs that continue after their original meaning is lost (for example, 
throwing rice or shoes at a wedding) prove earlier stages. 
Major evolutionist thinkers 
(a) Herbert Spencer (1820–1903) 
An English philosopher who applied evolution to society before Darwin's book. He compared 
society to a living organism that grows from simple to complex and coined the phrase "survival 
of the fittest". His ideas are sometimes called Social Darwinism. He believed societies develop 
from military (fighting) types to industrial (trading) types. Main work: The Principles of 
Sociology (1876–96). 
(b) Lewis Henry Morgan (1818–1881) 
An American lawyer and anthropologist who studied the Iroquois Indians and wrote about 
kinship. In Ancient Society (1877) he divided human history into three big periods, each with 
sub-stages, based mainly on technology and subsistence (how people get food).

Contributions of Evolutionism 
• Made the study of human society systematic and scientific. 
• Introduced the ideas of culture, kinship systems and the comparative method. 
• Showed that human institutions (family, religion, property, law) change over time. 
• Encouraged collection of data about tribal societies from around the world. 
• Fought the old belief that some races were separately created or permanently inferior; 
stressed the psychic unity of mankind. 
Criticisms of Evolutionism 
1. Armchair method: most evolutionists never did fieldwork. They relied on second-hand 
and sometimes unreliable reports.

2. Ethnocentrism: they placed European society at the top and called others "primitive" or 
"savage" – a biased judgement. 
3. Speculation: stages such as universal "promiscuity" or "matriarchy" had little proof. 
4. One-line path is false: societies do not all follow the same sequence. Some skip stages; 
some go backward; some develop in unique ways. 
5. Living fossils is wrong: every present-day society has its own long history; tribal 
societies are not "the past frozen in time". 
6. Neglect of history and diffusion: ignoring borrowing between societies (the point made 
by Diffusionists). 
7. Racist misuse: Social Darwinism was used to justify colonial rule and inequality. 
Neo-Evolutionism (a later revival) 
In the 20th century, scholars such as Leslie White, Julian Steward and Marshall Sahlins revived 
evolutionary ideas in a more careful form. White linked cultural progress to energy use per 
person; Steward proposed multilinear evolution (many paths, not just one) and stressed 
adaptation to environment. These are called neo-evolutionists.

Diffusionism 
Meaning of Diffusionism 
Diffusion means "spreading". Diffusionism is the theory that cultural traits (tools, ideas, 
customs, technologies) are invented in only one or a few places and then spread to other 
societies through contact, migration, trade and conquest. So the similarities we see between 
distant societies are mainly due to borrowing, not independent invention. 
Example: the spread of papermaking from China to the Arab world and then to Europe; the 
spread of tea, cotton, printing, the numerals 0–9 and the idea of zero from Asia to other parts 
of the world; the spread of mobile phones and UPI-like payment ideas in the modern age.

Merits (strengths) of Diffusionism 
 
• Correctly showed that contact and borrowing are major causes of cultural change – no 
society develops in isolation. 
• Gave importance to history, geography and migration. 
• Helped culture area studies and museum classification. 
• Encouraged the careful use of evidence (criteria of form and quantity). 
• Corrected the one-line picture of Evolutionism by showing many routes of 
development. 
Criticisms of Diffusionism

1. Extreme claims: believing one place (Egypt) was the source of all civilisations is 
unscientific and belittles other peoples. 
2. Ignores independent invention: similar things can arise separately (for example, the 
pyramids of Egypt and Mexico were built for distinct reasons at different times). 
3. Cannot explain why a trait is accepted or rejected – it only says, "it spread". 
4. Lack of written history: for non-literate societies, the routes of spread are guessed, not 
proved.

5. Neglects internal factors: how a society changes a borrowed trait to suit itself (called 
reinterpretation or acculturation). Treats culture as a heap of traits rather than a system 
of connected parts.

Functionalism 
Meaning 
Functionalism is the theory that every custom, belief and institution in a society has a function 
– a job it performs – that helps satisfy human needs or keeps society running smoothly. To 
understand any social practice, we must ask: what purpose does it serve and how is it connected 
to the rest of society? 
An easy comparison is the human body: the heart pumps blood, the lungs give oxygen, the 
kidneys clean the blood. Each organ has a function, and the body survives because they work 
together. In the same way, family, economy, religion, law and education are like "organs" of 
society.

Merits of Functionalism 
• Established intensive fieldwork as the core method. 
• Studied societies as wholes, showing the links between economy, religion, kinship and 
politics. 
• Replaced speculative history with observable facts. 
• Treated so-called "primitive" societies as rational and orderly, not backward. 
• Its ideas are useful to understand organisations (each department has a function) and 
institutions. 
Criticisms of Functionalism 
1. Static: it explains stability but not social change, conflict, or history. 
2. Overemphasis on harmony treats society as always balanced; ignores inequality, 
exploitation and power struggle (Marxist criticism). 
3. Teleological reasoning: says a custom exists "because" it serves a function – but a 
custom may have a function without being the reason it started. 
4. Difficult to test: any custom can be given some function by clever argument. 
5. Ignores the individual and meaning especially in Radcliffe-Brown, who treated people 
as parts of a system. 
6. Ignores colonial context: fieldwork was done within colonial rule, whose impact was 
often ignored. 
7. Evaluation problem: it fails to explain harmful (dysfunctional) customs.

Structuralism – Claude Lévi-Strauss 
Meaning of Structuralism 
Structuralism is the approach that looks for deep, hidden structures underlying the visible 
surface of culture. It holds that the many customs, myths, kinship rules and rituals we observe 
are like the "surface" of an iceberg; the real pattern lies below, in the way the human mind 
organises the world. 
Think of the grammar of a language. People speak fluently without knowing grammar rules, 
yet the rules shape every sentence. Structuralists believe that culture works like a language: it 
has an unseen "grammar" that we can discover. 
Claude Lévi-Strauss (1908–2009): life in brief 
Born in Brussels (Belgium) to French parents, he studied law and philosophy in Paris. In 1935 
he went to Brazil as a professor in São Paulo and did fieldwork among Amazonian peoples 
(Bororo, Nambikwara, Caduveo). During the Second World War he lived in New York, where 
he met Roman Jakobson, a linguist, and Franz Boas. He later held a chair in Social 
Anthropology at the Collège de France (from 1959) and became one of the most famous 
intellectuals of the 20th century. He lived to the age of 100.

Life and work 
S. F. Nadel (1903–1956) was born in Vienna, Austria. He first studied psychology, philosophy 
and music, then turned to anthropology under C. G. Seligman and Malinowski in London. 
Because of his training in logic and philosophy, he was known for clear, careful thought and

he became Professor of Anthropology at the Australian National University (Canberra) and

UNIT – III  
Kinship  
Introduction 
Kinship and religion are two of the most important institutions for understanding primitive 
and traditional societies. In societies where modern institutions such as formal government, 
courts, police, schools and welfare organizations were either absent or less developed, people 
depended heavily on family, kinship, customs, religion and traditional practices to organize 
their social life. Kinship provided the basic structure through which people established 
relationships, received protection, inherited property, regulated marriage and participated in 
economic activities. Religion provided beliefs, rituals and moral rules that helped people 
understand the natural and social world around them. Magic was also closely associated with 
religion and was often used to deal with uncertainty, danger and events that people could not 
explain through ordinary knowledge. 
 
Meaning of Kinship 
Kinship refers to the socially recognized relationships that exist between people on the basis 
of blood relationships, descent and marriage. In simple terms, kinship is a system of social 
relationships through which individuals are connected to one another as members of a family, 
lineage, clan or wider community. Relationships between parents and children, brothers and 
sisters, grandparents and grandchildren are examples of relationships based on descent or 
biological connection. Relationships such as husband and wife, father-in-law and daughter-
in-law, mother-in-law and son-in-law are established through marriage. However, kinship is 
not simply a biological relationship. Society gives these relationships particular rights, duties, 
responsibilities and expectations. For example, a father is not merely biologically related to 
his child but is also expected to provide care, protection and guidance. Similarly, relatives are 
often expected to help one another during marriage, illness, death and other important 
occasions. 
Kinship was particularly important in primitive societies because the individual was strongly 
connected with the family and wider kin group. A person's identity, social position, 
responsibilities and even economic opportunities were often determined by their membership 
in a particular family, lineage or clan. Instead of depending mainly on formal institutions, 
individuals often depended upon their relatives for protection, economic assistance and social 
security. Thus, kinship can be understood as one of the fundamental principles through which 
primitive societies were organized. 
 Importance of Kinship in Primitive Societies 
Kinship played a very important role in the organization of primitive societies. It provided the 
basic framework for social organization by bringing individuals together into families, 
lineages, clans and tribes. In many traditional societies, an individual was not viewed as an 
isolated person but as a member of a particular kin group. The behaviour of one individual

could affect the reputation and position of the entire family or clan. Therefore, kinship 
created a strong sense of belonging and collective identity. 
Kinship also played an important role in providing economic cooperation. Members of a kin 
group often worked together in activities such as hunting, fishing, agriculture, gathering food 
and constructing houses. When one member faced economic difficulty, other relatives could 
provide assistance. In this way, kinship acted as an informal system of economic security. 
The sharing of food, labour and other resources helped the community survive, particularly in 
situations where resources were uncertain. 
Kinship was also connected with political organization. In many traditional societies, 
leadership was associated with particular families, lineages or clans. Elders and influential 
members of kin groups could exercise authority and participate in decision-making. In some 
communities, disputes were settled through elders or representatives of the concerned 
families rather than through formal courts. Thus, kinship could provide a basis for political 
authority and conflict resolution. 
Another important function of kinship was social control. Members of a family or clan were 
expected to follow established customs and traditions. A person who violated social norms 
could bring shame not only upon themselves but also upon their family. The fear of losing 
social respect and the desire to maintain family honour encouraged individuals to follow 
accepted rules. Kinship therefore helped maintain discipline and social order. 
Kinship was also important in regulating marriage. Societies generally have rules concerning 
whom a person can marry and whom they cannot marry. Restrictions on marriage between 
close relatives are commonly found in human societies. At the same time, certain kinship 
systems encourage marriage between particular groups. Marriage therefore does not merely 
unite two individuals; it can also create relationships between two families, lineages or 
communities. 
Inheritance is another important area connected with kinship. Property, land, livestock, 
family possessions and social positions may be transferred according to rules of descent. In a 
patrilineal system, inheritance may traditionally pass through the male line, whereas in a 
matrilineal system descent and certain forms of inheritance are associated with the maternal 
line. Thus, kinship determines not only personal relationships but also access to material 
resources. 
Kinship also performs an important emotional and psychological function. Relatives provide 
companionship, affection, care and support during difficult situations. During events such as 
birth, marriage, illness and death, relatives come together and provide practical and emotional 
assistance. In this sense, kinship provides a feeling of security and belonging. 
 
 Types of Kinship 
The family is generally regarded as the most basic kinship group. It consists of individuals 
connected through marriage, descent, adoption or socially recognized relationships. The

family performs important functions such as reproduction, socialization, economic 
cooperation, protection and emotional support. In primitive societies, the family was often 
closely connected with wider kinship groups. 
A lineage is a kinship group whose members believe that they can trace their descent from a 
known common ancestor. Members of a lineage may share property, participate in common 
rituals and cooperate in economic and social activities. A clan is generally a larger kinship 
group whose members claim descent from a common ancestor, although the exact 
genealogical connection may not always be known. In some societies, the common ancestor 
of a clan may be represented by an animal, plant or natural object. This relationship is 
sometimes connected with the concept of totemism. 
A phratry refers to a larger social group consisting of several related clans. A moiety refers to 
a division of a society into two major social groups. Each group may have its own rules, 
rituals and responsibilities. These forms of kinship organization demonstrate that traditional 
societies could have complex systems of social organization even when they did not have 
modern political institutions. 
 
 Affinal Kinship: Affinal kinship is the term used to describe the relationship between two 
people who are married. When a person marries, he forms a bond with not only the girl he 
marries, but also several other members of her family. Furthermore, not only the person 
marrying is tied to the girl's family, but so are his family members. As a result, when a couple 
marries, a slew of new relationships is born. A person becomes not only a husband after 
marriage, but also a brother in- law and a son-in-law. It's worth noting that several marriage-
related relationships are referred to by the same term in the English language. Sala, jija, and 
other in-laws are all referred to as "brother-in-law." A person's name changes to foofa, 
nandoi, and mausa after they marry.  Similarly, when a girl marries, she not only becomes a 
wife but also a daughter-in-law; she is known as chichi, bhabhi, devrani, jethani, mami, and 
so on. As a result, marriage gives rise to a slew of affinal kin relationships.  
 Consanguineous Kinship: Consanguineous kinship refers to the relationship between 
people who are related by blood. Consanguineous kin are blood relatives, whereas affinal kin 
are married relatives.  
Consanguineous kinship describes the relationship between parents and their children, as well 
as siblings. Consanguineous kinship is kinship between brothers and sisters. Children of the 
same parents are known as siblings. Sons, brothers, sisters, uncles, elder uncles, nephews, and 
cousins are all consanguineous relatives. i.e. they're blood relatives. It should be noted that a 
blood relationship can be both real and imagined in this context. The father of a child is 
unknown among polyandrous tribes. A biologically produced child is treated as if it were 
one's own. As a result, blood relations can be established not only biologically, but also 
socially.

Family  
The family is the fundamental unit of all human societies, regardless of its nature. The family 
is the foundation of all human societies, whether primitive or modern. It can be found in 
some form or another in all cultures and groups.  
 Family is a group of persons united by the ties of marriage, blood, or adoption, consisting of 
a single household, interacting and intercommunicating with each other in their respective 
roles  of husband and wife, mother and father, son and daughter, brother and sister, and 
creating and maintaining a common culture.  
Functions of Family  
A family is a functional unit among tribes, as it is in any society. It serves certain functions 
for both its members and society. Family functions can be divided into two categories: Basic 
and Traditional.  
a) Basic Functions  
i. Biological Functions: Include sexual needs fulfilment, reproduction, and so on. These are 
regarded as critical functions.  
ii. Psychological Functions: Include child protection and rearing, wife safety and security, 
and so on. Family is not only a place of birth but also a place of protection and care for 
children.  
b) Traditional Functions  
i. Economic Functions: It includes meeting its members’ economic needs such as food, 
clothing, and shelter. A member or members of the family arrange for the family’s livelihood. 
They also create and maintain family property. 
ii. Social Functions: These functions include child socialization for personality development 
and education. Members learn about their culture through socialization. The family shapes 
the behavior of its members based on culture. As a result, the family is an important agency 
for transmitting culture to the next generation.  
iii. Religious and Cultural Functions: The family teaches its members about religion. The 
family teaches children about their customs, traditions, taboos, art, music, and dancing.  
iv. Health Related Functions: The family is concerned about the health of its members. It also 
teaches them about the tribal system of medicine, which is primarily based on 
herbs.  However, they believe in magic, witchcraft, sorcery, and other supernatural cures 
because they believe that evil spirits cause diseases.  
v. Organizational Functions: The tribal family is the primary organizational unit in the 
village.  Each family contributes money, labor, and personnel to the village’s well-being.  
Finally, it aids in efficiently utilizing the environment, which is required to satisfy man’s 
more intimate needs, such as hunger.  
 
Characteristics of Tribal Family

• A family is limited in size.  
• The relationship between family members is permanent.  
• Husband and wife are inseparable sexual partners.  
• At least one family member must be the breadwinner for all members. • Members live in the 
same house.  
• Members use the same nomenclature.  
• The family is the primary source of education for children.  
 
Classification of the Family  
Based on Marriage  
i. Monogamous Family: A monogamous family consists of one husband and one wife. The 
monogamous family system is a very common type of family among the tribes. 
ii. Polygynous Family: A polygynous family is one in which a man marries more than one 
wife. Polygynous families are common throughout tribal India. This type of family can be 
found among the Nagas and Gonds, as well as in Odisha’s tribes.  
iii. Polyandrous Family: It is made up of one woman and several husbands. Two types of 
polyandrous families are 
 (i) Fraternal polyandry  
 (ii) Non-Fraternal polyandry.  
In fraternal polyandry, a woman’s husbands are brothers. The Khasis practice this type of 
family. In non-fraternal polyandry, a woman’s husbands are not related to each other.  
Based on Structure  
i. Nuclear Family: It is made up of both the couple and their unmarried children. These 
families include the Khasi, Juang, Santhal, and Bhuinya.  
ii. A joint family comprises closely related relatives or two or more nuclear families. It could 
be either matrilocal or patrilocal. This type of family can be found among several Indian 
tribes.  
iii. Extended Family: The extended family is formed when the addition of closely related kin 
expands the nuclear family. It comprises aunts, grandparents, grandchildren, and so on. As  a 
result, an extended family is very large. These families are common among the Santhal, Ho. 
Juang, and others.  
Based on Residence  
i. Patrilocal Family: When a couple moves to live with the husband’s family after marriage, 
the family is known as a patrilocal family. The patrilocal family system is a common type of 
family among the Oraon, Ho, and Kharia tribes.

ii. Matrilocal Family: After marriage, the husband moves into the wife’s home and lives 
there.  The Khasi, for example, have a matrilocal family.  
 
Based on Authority  
i. Patriarchal Family: The father wields absolute power in this type of family. Patriarchal 
families are common in the majority of Indian tribes. 
ii. Matriarchal Family: A matriarchal family is one in which authority is held by the mother 
or any of the female members of the household. The Khasi tribe is one example.  
iii. Avunculocal Family: When the sources of authority are neither father nor mother but 
uncle, it is called avaunculocal units.  
 
Based on Ancestry and Property Inheritance  
i. Patrilineal Family: A patrilineal family is one in which descent is traced through the father, 
and property inheritance occurs along the male line of descent. This type of family is found in 
a variety of tribes.  
ii. Matrilineal Family: A matrilineal family is one in which descent is traced through the 
mother and females inherit property. Assam’s Garo and Khasi families are two examples of 
this type of family.  
Based on Blood Relationship  
i. Consanguineous Family: A nucleus of blood relatives is surrounded by a fringe of spouses 
to form this type of family. In other words, the consanguineous family comprises primary 
families and blood relatives. It is made up of members who are related by blood. Marriage 
does not end in this type of family, and family membership continues even after 
marriage.  This type of family can be found among the Khasis of Assam and Meghalaya.  
ii. Conjugal Family: This type of family consists of a husband, wife, and their children, as 
well as their affinal kin. The conjugal bond is highlighted in this family. The conjugal family 
is found in the majority of Indian tribes. As an example, consider the Kharia family of Orissa 
and Chotanagpur.  
Meaning of Religion 
Religion is a system of beliefs, values, rituals and practices related to the sacred or 
supernatural. It attempts to provide explanations about important questions concerning 
human existence, life, death, nature, suffering and the unknown. Religion can involve belief 
in gods, spirits, ancestors or other supernatural powers. It can also involve sacred places, 
objects, symbols, ceremonies and moral rules. 
Religion was particularly important in primitive societies because people often faced natural 
events that they could not explain scientifically. Thunder, lightning, drought, floods, disease, 
death, dreams and changes in seasons could create fear and uncertainty. Religious beliefs and

rituals provided explanations for such events and gave people a framework for understanding 
their environment. 
Theories of the Origin of Religion 
Sociologists and anthropologists have proposed different theories to explain the origin and 
development of religion. Two major approaches relevant to this topic are the evolutionary 
approach and the functional approach. The evolutionary approach attempts to understand how 
religious beliefs may have developed over time, while the functional approach focuses more 
on the functions performed by religion in society. 
 Evolutionary Theory of Religion 
The evolutionary approach developed mainly during the nineteenth century. Scholars such as 
E.B. Tylor, James Frazer, Herbert Spencer and R.R. Marett attempted to explain religion as 
something that developed gradually as human beings tried to understand their environment 
and their own experiences. 
E.B. Tylor considered animism to be an important early form of religion. According to Tylor, 
early human beings experienced dreams, death, sleep and visions and attempted to explain 
these experiences through the idea of the soul or spirit. For example, when a person dreamed 
about someone who was physically absent, early humans might have interpreted this as 
evidence that the person's spirit could exist separately from the physical body. From this kind 
of reasoning, beliefs in souls and spirits could develop. Tylor therefore associated early 
religious thought with the belief that supernatural spirits existed in humans, animals and 
aspects of nature. 
James Frazer proposed an evolutionary sequence involving magic, religion and science. In his 
classical formulation, human beings initially attempted to control nature through magic. 
When magical practices were considered insufficient, people increasingly turned towards 
supernatural beings through religion. With the development of observation, experimentation 
and rational knowledge, science eventually developed as another means of understanding 
nature. This idea can be summarized as Magic → Religion → Science. Contemporary 
anthropology does not generally accept this as a universal sequence through which every 
society necessarily passes, but Frazer's theory remains historically important in the study of 
anthropology and religion. 
Herbert Spencer emphasized ancestor worship in explaining the development of religion. 
According to this approach, experiences involving death, dreams and memories of deceased 
relatives could encourage people to believe that the dead continued to exist in spiritual form. 
These spirits could then be regarded as capable of influencing the living. Religious practices 
could consequently develop around the remembrance and worship of ancestors. 
R.R. Marett proposed the concept of animatism to describe belief in an impersonal 
supernatural power. According to this idea, early people might believe that certain objects, 
places or individuals possessed special supernatural power. Such beliefs demonstrate that 
religion does not necessarily begin with clearly defined gods or spirits but can also involve 
more general ideas about supernatural power. 
Functional Theory of Religion

The functional approach does not primarily ask how religion originated. Instead, it asks what 
religion does for individuals and society. Important scholars associated with this approach 
include Émile Durkheim, Bronislaw Malinowski and A.R. Radcliffe-Brown. 
Émile Durkheim studied religion as a social institution. In his work The Elementary Forms of 
Religious Life, he examined religious life among Australian Aboriginal communities as 
represented in the ethnographic material available to him. Durkheim argued that religion 
creates social solidarity by bringing people together around shared beliefs, symbols and 
rituals. He distinguished between the sacred and the profane. The sacred refers to things that 
are considered special, holy or set apart, while the profane refers to ordinary everyday 
activities and objects. 
According to Durkheim, religious rituals bring people together and create a sense of 
collective belonging. During collective ceremonies, people may experience intense emotional 
energy and a feeling of being part of something larger than themselves. Durkheim described 
this experience as collective effervescence. Religious symbols can therefore become symbols 
of the community itself and strengthen social solidarity. 
Bronislaw Malinowski emphasized the role of religion and magic in dealing with uncertainty 
and psychological stress. According to Malinowski, human beings may have technical 
knowledge for dealing with ordinary situations, but uncertainty remains in activities 
involving danger and unpredictable outcomes. For example, a fisherman may possess 
considerable knowledge about fishing but may still perform rituals before entering dangerous 
waters. Such rituals can provide confidence, courage and emotional security. 
A.R. Radcliffe-Brown emphasized the relationship between religion, ritual and social 
structure. According to this approach, religious rituals can strengthen social relationships and 
reinforce shared values. Rituals help individuals recognize their obligations towards one 
another and contribute to the maintenance of social order. 
Marriage  
Marriage is a social institution and marriage and family are complementary concepts. As such 
marriage is found in almost all societies. Without marriage one cannot think of a family. 
“Marriage is, “a set of cultural patterns to sanction parenthood and to provide a stable 
background for the care and rearing of children.” 
The Tribal Marriages can be classified into the following types:  
1. Monogamy: In this type of marriage one man married to one woman or one woman 
marries one man. The husband and wife may or may not be (usually not) related to each other 
before marriage, most of the Indian tribes practice monogamy.  
2. Polygamy:  
It is the marriage of one person with more than one person of the opposite sex. It has two 
subtypes:  
(a) Polygyny.  
(b) Polyandry.

(a) Polygyny:  
In this type of marriage one man marries several women. The husband and wives may or may 
not be related to each other before marriage. Wives may be related among themselves. When 
the wives are related to each other as sisters it is called sororal polygyny. If they are not 
related as sisters, it is called non-sororal polygyny. Polygyny is found among the Naga tribes, 
the Gond, the Baiga and the Toda. It is also found among the Lushai, Juang and the Kondh.  
Polygyny is practiced among the tribals due to several reasons. First of all, it is practiced due 
to the imbalance of the sex ratio, where women outnumber men. The second reason is that the 
practice of polygyny accords higher status and prestige. This is the reason why the tribal 
chiefs keep many wives. Thirdly the tribals like the Lushai or the Gonds practice polygyny. 
So that a number of wives and their children will provide the husband with free and reliable 
labor.  
 
Merits of Polygyny:  
 
Polygyny has the following merits:  
(i) It facilitates better division of labor in the family.  
(ii) It ensures the adequate sexual satisfaction of the husband.  
(iii) It reproduces a number of strong children born to the wives of physically strong men.  
The following are the demerits, of polygyny:  
(i) It makes the family a center of quarrel and spoils family peace.  
(ii) The status of women suffers a serious setback in a polygynous family due to the presence 
of several wives. 
(iii) Children are not properly looked after in the polygynous family.  
(iv) It lacks in better understanding, fellow feeling, sympathy, love and affection among the 
co wives.  
(v) It is also disadvantageous from the economic point of view.  
(vi) It snatches away the conjugal love and psychological satisfaction from women.  
(vii) It causes jealousy and suspicion and family instability due to lack of proper 
understanding among spouses and offspring.  
 
(b) Polyandry:  
In polyandry type of marriage, one woman married to several men. The wife and the 
husbands may or may not be related to each other before marriage. The husbands may be 
related among themselves. If the husbands are all brothers, then this marriage is called 
fraternal polyandry. If the husbands are not related to each other and share the same wife, it is

called non-fraternal polyandry.  Polyandry as a form of marriage is very much restricted and 
is confined to a few tribal communities, mostly along the foothills of the Himalayas. The 
Kota, the Khasa, the Toda, the Ladani Bota and the Khasi practice this type of marriage. 
There is evidence to establish the fact that some pre-Dravidian and Dravidian tribes practiced 
Polyandry.  
Fraternal Polyandry (Adelphic):  
The Todas of Nilgiris hills and the Khasa practices fraternal polyandry. The elder brother 
marries his wife and according to this practice of Adelphic, she becomes the wife of all the 
brothers. She is shared by all the brothers of a family for satisfaction of sexual urges. The 
minor brothers of the family become her husband after being major. But the elder brother 
becomes the father of all her children.  
Non-Fraternal Polyandry (Non-Adelphic):  
In this form of marriage, a woman marries many men who are not necessarily brothers. She 
satisfies their sexual desire. By turn, going from one husband to another. The husbands may 
either live in one place or in different places. During her life with one husband, that particular 
husband enjoys her exclusively for that particular period and others do not have their right at 
that time. The Nayar women practice non- fraternal polyandry and constitute a matriarchal 
family.  
Polyandry is practiced due to several reasons. The imbalance in sex ratio, less number of 
females of marriageable age is another reason. The poor practices polyandry whereas the rich 
can afford to practise polygyny. Fraternal polyandry is often preferred to keep the family 
property undivided because, it does not allow the brothers to marry separate wives and live 
with them in separate  
households. Higher Bride price may be considered as another cause of polyandry. When the 
husbands are unable to pay the bride price individually, they may prefer polyandry to 
monogamy.  
Bigamy:  
In Mysore, the Medara and Holiya tribes practise bigamy type of marriage wherein a male is 
allowed to marry two women at a time. The co-wives are related as sisters.  
 
Preference & Prohibition in Tribal Marriage:  
All societies have rule and restrictions about whom one may or may not marry. This is 
referred to as the system of prohibition or encouragement or preference of the choice of male 
in marriage.  Madan & Majumdar write that “All over India, and in other parts of the world 
as well, we come across rules laying down prohibitions, preferences and prescriptions in 
deciding the form of marriage.”  
There are certain categories of relatives who come within the prohibitory degree of marital 
relationship. There are also some other relatives with whom sexual relationship is prohibited. 
“A Taboo on sexual relationship between closely related kin like parents and children and 
between siblings is universal.

An extension of this “nuclear prohibition” is found everywhere. Therefore, among several 
tribal communities we find the practice of marrying outside the family, clan, village etc. 
Violation of this restriction is seriously dealt with. The practice of marrying outside one’s 
own family clan, village or group is called as Exogamy. Among the Indian tribes we also find 
another peculiar practice of marrying within one’s own group. This marriage within one’s 
own group is known as Endogamy. The Victorian Anthropologist MacLennan had coined 
these two terms, which simply meant marrying in and marrying out.  
(a) Family Exogamy:  
Marriage outside the family.  
(b) Clan exogamy:  
Marriage outside the clan.  
(c) Village Exogamy:  
Marriage outside the village. The practice of clan exogamy is widely followed among the 
Indian tribals like Gond, the Baiga, the Ho, the Korwa, the Khasi, the Nagadsoon. The 
Munda tribe of Chhotanagpur region practise village exogamy. 
Tracing the cause of Exogamy, Audrey Richards has pointed out that “in hunting and food 
gathering societies, food is difficult to obtain. Women and children are generally a burden in 
such societies, particularly those which rely more on hunting. This could have led to female 
infanticide, which in consequence, would lead to female scarcity. This must have led to 
marriage by capture, and the next step-since such capture had to be affected from outside the 
tribe to exogamy. Thus, food scarcity may be, historically speaking a probable cause of 
exogamy.”  
Endogamy:  
Majumdar and Madan say that the practice of marrying within one’s own tribe or very rarely 
the clan is called endogamy.  
Thus, mainly, we find two types of endogamies:  
(a) Clan endogamy—Marriage within the clan.  
(b) Tribe endogamy — Marriage within the tribe.  
The Todas of Nigiri Hills have two main clans such as Tartharol and the Teivaliol. These 
clans are endogamous groups, but their subdivisions and sibs practise exogamy. Likewise, the 
Bhils have two endogamous groups such as-the Uyale Bhil and the Mele Bhil. Most of the 
tribes are clan exogamous but phratry and tribe endogamous. However, now-a-days, some 
sophisticated tribes in India like the Gond, the Bhil and the Santhal have broken down the 
barriers of endogamy and have started marrying with the lower castes, for their incorporation 
into the Hindu castes.  
A number of causes may be given in support of the practice of endogamy:

(a) Universal fear of the stronger, unknown and the novel- Generally the tribals are afraid of 
the neighbour’s witchcraft and sorcery. The Korwa tribe practices endogamy particularly on 
account of that reason.  
(b) Territorial and Linguistic Factors-Territorial and linguistic factors “impose limits on the 
communication of thoughts and persons (Spouses) between various groups.”  
(c) Desire to preserve the socio-cultural identity-Each tribal group possesses its own 
distinctive socio-cultural identity, sharing enough thought and action pattern. Which they 
want to preserve through the practice of endogamy.  
Preferential Marriages:  
In certain cases, there is a prescription expressed for establishing martial ties with a particular 
kin or preferences designed to promote inter-familiar cordiality by making certain linkages 
imperative.  Such marriages are known as preferential marriages. 
The tribes in India practise the following types of preferential marriages: (a) Cousin 
marriage.  
(i) Cross cousin marriage.  
(ii) Parallel cousin marriage.  
(b) Levirate  
(i) Junior Levirate.  
(ii) Senior Levirate.  
(c) Sororate.  
Cousin Marriage:  
The Gond, the Kharia, the Oraon, the Khasi, and the Kadar practice cousin marriage. The 
cousin marriages can be sub- divided into:  
(i) Cross-cousin marriage and  
(ii) parallel cousin marriage.  
The marriage between mother’s brother’s (Maternal uncle’s) children and father’s sister’s 
(paternal aunt’s) children is called cross cousin marriage. Majumdar and Madan hold that 
“cross-cousin marriage as a form of exogamy, the only form of exogamy under dual 
organization, is often explained to be a device for avoiding payment of a high bride price and 
also for maintaining property in the household”.  
Cross Cousin marriage is found among different tribes in southern India. The Gonds of 
Madhya Pradesh practice cross-cousin marriage and call it; ‘dudhlautawa’ or the ‘return of 
milk’. This is called so because the bride price paid by the husband for his wife comes back 
to his own family through the marriage of his daughter with the son of his wife’s brother. 
Marrying one’s father’s brother’s child or mother’s sister’s child is called a parallel cousin 
marriage. The main purpose of preferential mating, according to Levi-Strauss, is to 
strengthen the solidarity of a tribal group.

Levirate:  
Sometimes, preferential marriages also aim at solidifying the inter-family unity. If a man 
dies, his wife is inherited by the brother of the deceased husband. This practice of being 
actual or potential mates to one’s husband's brother is called levirate. The custom of Levirate 
is found among several tribes like Santal, Ho, Saora, Bhuinya, Munda etc. Marriage of the 
widow with the deceased  
husband’s elder brother is called senior Levirate. But when she married the younger brother 
of the dead husband, it was called junior Levirate.  
Levirate as a form of marriage is useful for tribal society. First of all, it allows widow 
remarriage.  Secondly it provides the widow with social security within the same family. 
Thirdly it also provides social security to the offspring of the widow which is not possible in 
other types of widow remarriage. Fourthly it strengthens the solidarity between inter-family 
unity.  
Sororate:  
The practice of being actual or potential mates to one’s wife’s sisters is called sororate. 
Majumdar and Madan hold that “when several sisters are simultaneously or potentially, the 
spouses of the same man the practice is called sororate. The death of a spouse is compensated 
by supplying a new spouse, generally a younger brother of the deceased ''. The custom of 
Sororate is found among the tribal communities where the practice of bride-price is prevalent. 
Sororate also recognizes marriage as a tie between two families and lays emphasis on the 
acceptance of inter- familial obligations.  
Positive sanction in Tribal Marriage:  
The following types of marriage in the tribal societies are accorded positive sanction: (a) 
Tribe endogamy.  
(b) Clan exogamy.  
(c) Preferential Mating.  
The tribe exogamy, clan endogamy (incest) are looked down upon, pre-marital or post-
marital sexual relationship is not uncommon among tribal societies in India Indulgences in 
this kind of sexual activities is possible even without the displeasure of the society because 
pre-marital chastity is not stressed in marriages. The tribes living in the central India do not 
view pre-marital relationship seriously unless that leads to pregnancy. If it results in 
pregnancy, the male partner is compelled to marry the pregnant girl.  
In the Bastar district of Madhya Pradesh, the Muria Gonds allow the bachelors and Maiden to 
sleep in a common dormitory. They are free to indulge in pairing off in the dormitory. The 
Orans, the Khaddi, and the Hos indulge in pairing off activities on important festivals like 
Magha-parab, among the Konyak Nagas a girl may indulge in pre-marital sex till she 
becomes a mother. The Khas allow pre- marital sex but strictly prohibit any extra-marital 
sexual relationship for the wives. 
Religion:

Tribal religion is based on oral traditions. The tribes express their beliefs in everyday 
language.  Their rituals are aimed at solving day to day problems of life. Objects of worship 
are things of nature such as trees, rivers, mountain, sun, moon and earth. Rituals are mostly 
performed collectively and transmitted orally.  
Tribal World view is grounded in the natural events and life-experiences. Their cosmology is 
socially effective i.e. existential, but un-interpretative.  
Faith in supernatural is structured in a tribal society. According to the 1961 census of India, it 
would appear that about 89 per cent of the tribals claimed to profess Hinduism and 5 per cent 
had converted to Christianity. Most of the tribals in India follow some or other form of 
Hinduism. It is mainly due to the contacts the tribals had with their Hindu neighbors. 
Christianity was introduced among the tribal groups during the British rule.  
Almost all the tribal religions across India believe in the existence of spiritual powers. The 
most important problem of life is to deal with these powers to ensure individual and 
collective well-being. The solution for this is to seek conciliation and communion with the 
more definite and potent personal spirits and to deal with the more indefinite and impersonal 
forces by way of control, expulsion or avoidance through appropriate rites, ceremonies, spells 
and taboos.  
Religion of a tribe is simple. Religious beliefs and behavior are not treated as something apart 
from other kinds of beliefs and behavior. Religion pervades all aspects of their life. Tribal life 
and society cannot be fully understood without understanding their religion.  
Tribal Religion in a state of simplicity:  
Religion of a tribe is simple insofar as it is expressed in everyday language and experienced 
in everyday life. Every tribal religious system consists of three essential elements. Firstly, 
they believe in the existence of a superhuman world which refers to the belief system of 
tribals. Secondly, they form a human relationship to the superhuman world which refers to 
their value system. Thirdly for establishing a relationship they practice various rites and 
rituals which refer to their action system.  
The tribals believe the superhuman world as the real world. They communicate to this world 
through symbolic words called the ritual language.  
Forms of ritual may vary from one tribe to another, but the basic ritual code of Mantra, 
Mudra, Dhvani, and Vyavahariki is applicable to all cultures.   
Mantras are simple words of everyday language used by tribes in the performance of their 
rites and rituals. 
Mudras are various kinds of hand gestures and bodily positions representing specific feelings 
and esoteric actions. In tribal dance the movement of steps, interlocking of hands and other 
hand gestures have both aesthetic and ritualistic significance.  
Dhvani is the third component of ritual language. The sound of musical instrument guides the 
dance Mudra. Certain forms of sound have special significance.  
In course of the performance of a ritual what follows in the form of prescriptions or 
instructions, thoughts, methods and behaviour is the vyavahariki code.

Religion and Magic  
We can see the effect of religion and magic in any primitive and modern, developed and 
undeveloped society and culture. There is no visible society and culture in which the presence 
of these two aspects (religion and magic) is not targeted. Even in today's advanced religious 
societies, the presence of magical actions is targeted. In both rural and urban areas of India, 
there are tricks and sorcery along with religious activities. Similarly, in primitive cultures 
there is a predominance of magic rituals, we can see many religious rituals being performed 
in their original form.  
Therefore, it would not be untrue to say that both religion and magic have equal importance 
in the field of day-to-day social life and both prove helpful in nurturing different aspects of 
life.  Nevertheless, here we have to accept that in societies and cultures in which science is 
relatively underdeveloped, the predominance of religion and magic is more than in developed 
societies and cultures. Science and scientific approaches tend to explain phenomena logically 
and thus reduce the need for non-rational methods.  
The beliefs and beliefs generated by this experience can develop in two different directions. 
If a person accepts his incapacity and bows before these supernatural powers and starts 
worshiping them and considering himself dependent on him and surrenders to him, then the 
feeling which is created in it is called religion. On the contrary, when these supernatural 
forces are tried to be subdued and controlled then it is called magic.  
Magic: Conceptual Analysis   
Magic is such a process of practical actions by which supernatural powers are controlled with 
the help of some special mystical and secret techniques and methods and attempts are made 
to fulfil the desired cosmic desires.  
In order to make magic clearer, it is necessary to note their following characteristics:   
1. Magic is such a process of practical activities, under which various types of mystical and 
occult techniques and methods, such as mantras etc. are used.   
2. By the use of these techniques and methods, the desired worldly objectives are fulfilled.   
3. The fulfilment of these specific goals is considered to be coercive, because under it efforts 
are made to gain control over supernatural powers.   
4. In this, an attempt is made to please the supernatural powers in a mystical way.   
5. Religious prayers and praise are also sometimes used in magic. In the field of Hindu 
religion, it is believed that if a person chants Mahamrityunjaya by a virtuous person, then for 
some time victory over death can be achieved. Along with this, it is also believed that if one 
chants Mahamrityunjaya in reverse:   
If one does or gets it done in the name of one's enemy, the death of his enemy is inevitable. If 
a person with this thinking does the reverse chanting of Maha Mrityunjay in the context of 
causing harm to his enemy, then this act will be considered as a magical act and not as a 
religious act, because such accomplishment can be achieved only by following some specific 
techniques and methods. not supernatural power by the grace or grace of. This would prove

1. Use of certain techniques and methods  
Some special techniques and methods are used in magic activities. With the help of these 
techniques and methods, an attempt is made to influence the events that occur automatically. 
With the help of these, an attempt is made to liquefy the gods or supernatural powers. The 
users of specific techniques and methods have the belief that if certain programs are 
implemented in a subtle way, then certain results will definitely come out. Thus, the legal 
application is based on a preconceived notion of an overall regularity of cause and effect. The 
most important of the specific techniques and methods is the technique "Mantra". Mantras are 
words that are different from common words and are often kept secret. It is used only by 
those who do magic.  
2. With the use of Mantras of some specific physical equipment   
Some specific physical devices are necessarily used in the magic action. In this, essentially 
physical materials, such as soil, rice, mustard, skull, flower, wax, knife, hair, fingernail, 
betel, soap, thread, rope, flower, bean and other gross physical and atomic substances are 
used. It is believed that the supernatural cannot be forced to act according to will without the 
use of material factors.   
3. Mystical Behavior   
The performance of mystical behavior is considered essential for the achievement of the goal 
in the magic action of. The magician is seen performing many types of rituals to gain control 
over the supernatural power. In this context, he expresses a variety of emotional expressions 
in a dramatic manner. Often his body posture is situated in a specific posture. His state of 
mind is somewhat surprising and strange. Sometimes his form looks very frightening.   
4. Special costumes, costumes and ornaments  
There is a great need to wear special clothes and costumes in the magic action. Magicians 
generally use various colors to make their personality attractive. They are often required to 
wear coloured clothes like black, garrick and red etc. To make the body attractive, they are in 
addition to different types of coloured clothes. R's ornaments are also used. In the ears, they 
also use an ornament called Kundal and Karna Shobhan, and a string etc. in their hands. 
Often, they also wear gems around the neck. Kapir Jadar embellishes the hair itself by 
weaving it in various forms. In the fingers of the hands, they also often use rings made of 
materials.   
5. Prohibited Behavior   
Certain diets and types of behaviour are prohibited on the days when magical rituals are 
performed.  Not only this, but in those days, it is considered necessary to lead a different 
type of life from the normal life. If the desired effect is not achieved by the magic action, then 
it is often thought that the magician must have violated some prohibited practices in relation 
to its failure.

1. In both religion and magic, there is complete faith in getting the help of supernatural

2. Both of them are inspired by the mystery of creation.   
3. The core of both is contained in subjectivity.   
4. Both often serve a practical purpose.   
5. The sides of rituals and rituals are equally visible in both.   
6. Both are characterized by collective action.  
7. There is a certain less to be done to do both.   
8. In both, the need for a "virtuous" person is felt. In the field of religion, the role of a

9. In both religion and magic, certain mantras are kept secret.   
10. In both, certain foods and types of behavior are prohibited.   
11. It is believed in both that the combined effect of chants and actions brings closer to the

12. The reason for the failure of the intended goal in both is attributed to either an error in the 
word order of the mantras or the actions performed with them, or the violation of the
